extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator; literate early-18th-century public interested in morals, manners, and literature
extracted.subtask_description: Short moral and social essays (The Spectator-style) giving guidance and critique on character, conduct, and literary practice; includes illustrative letters, anecdotes, and allegories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honesty in character depiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets will attempt it with the Honesty which becomes their Characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters in plays and essays should be portrayed with honesty appropriate to their station; authors should avoid artifice that misrepresents moral make-up. The text contrasts earlier practice and praises Steele's plays for aiming at a 'wholesome influence upon his audience.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid spurious oaths and forced dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: Discarding the customary way of enforcing feeble dialogues by the spurious force of oaths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dramatic dialogue should not rely on coarse or artificial devices (oaths) to create force; instead aim for natural, morally edifying speech. Steele's practice of retrenching such passages is given as an example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compose complex characters combining noble virtues and agreeable qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: A Man that is Temperate, Generous, Valiant, Chaste, Faithful and Honest, may, at the same time, have Wit, Humour, Mirth, Good-breeding, and Gallantry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters should show a balance of moral virtues and social graces; authors should invent occasions to display these virtues so that they 'smite and reprove the Heart of a Man of Sense' and persuade readers toward virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide moral consequences at the catastrophe
rubrics_metrics.description: If at the Catastrophe he were found out for a Traitor, and met with Contempt accordingly?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When depicting wrongdoing, ensure the dramatic or narrative resolution exposes vice and accords just contempt or punishment—so the work reinforces moral lessons rather than excusing vice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy should satirize follies/types, not alienate the audience
rubrics_metrics.description: When people laughed at the paper, they laughed at the Idiot, the German Courtier, the Gaper, the Merry-Andrew, the Haberdasher, the Biter, the Butt, and not at [the reader].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humour that targets recognisable follies and character-types is defensible; avoid making the reader feel personally attacked. Successful comic writing mocks folly, not the audience's character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improve women by educating men's esteem (value virtue over beauty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Teach the Men not to be any longer dazzled by false Charms and unreal Beauty... it is worth the while to endeavour by all means to make them sensible that the Honour paid to them is only, upon account of their conducting themselves with Virtue, Modesty, and Discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To raise the moral and social status of women, reform male tastes and expectations: praise and reward modesty, virtue, and discretion rather than mere outward beauty; altering male esteem will encourage better conduct among women.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulate intercourse between sexes by honour and prudence
rubrics_metrics.description: Conversation between Ladies and Gentlemen, regulated by the Rules of Honour and Prudence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowing measured, honourable interaction between the sexes preserves wit and good manners; prohibiting all intercourse risks dulling women's wit and men's good-breeding. Social rules should aim to balance propriety with civil society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condemn ogling and peeping in public devotion
rubrics_metrics.description: A Peeper... works with her Hands, Eyes, and Fan... a Peeper as much more pernicious than a Starer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public behaviour—especially in solemn settings like divine service—should be modest: using gestures and artifice to attract looks (peeping, fan-play) is censured as more insidious than open staring and should be discouraged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use time productively; beware the 'Lowngers' (idleness)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Lowngers are... satisfied with being merely Part of the Number of Mankind, without distinguishing themselves... All they know of Life is only the present Instant, and do not taste even that.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay satirises a sect who 'kill time' rather than employ it; implicit prescription: students and men of letters should not squander time in listless wandering or mere show, but should cultivate study, writing, and useful observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Students and scholars should write and study, not merely promenade
rubrics_metrics.description: The ancients walked much, yet they wrote much also... Whereas it is notorious that most of our Professors never lay out a Farthing either in Pen, Ink, or Paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Academics should pair public life (walking, conversation) with productive labour—writing, study, and publication—rather than treating visibility or fashionable pastime as substitutes for learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the twin vices of Luxury and Avarice; prefer moderation
rubrics_metrics.description: When a Government flourishes in Conquests, and is secure from foreign Attacks, it naturally falls into all the Pleasures of Luxury... the two Principles of Action draw different Ways, Luxury... degenerates into Avarice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both excessive indulgence (luxury) and excessive greed (avarice) are corrupting; individuals and states should seek moderation. The allegory (two tyrants and their counsellors) warns that dismissing prudential counsellors leads to the two vices uniting in the same heart.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosperous governments should guard against luxury-driven corruption
rubrics_metrics.description: When the most formidable States of the World were subdued by the Romans, the Republic sunk into those two Vices of a quite different Nature, Luxury and Avarice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rulers and public institutions in times of peace and plenty are at special risk of moral decay; civic prudence and institutional checks are necessary to prevent the slide into vanity, corruption, and rapacity.
